segs.e: These are the five benefits of walking meditation.”
Numbered Discourses 5.30
3. With Five Factors
With Nāgita
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā kosalesu cārikaṁ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṁ yena icchānaṅgalaṁ nāma kosalānaṁ brāhmaṇagāmo tadavasari.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Icchānaṅgala.

segs.p: Tatra sudaṁ bhagavā icchānaṅgale viharati icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍe.
segs.e: He stayed in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.
The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard:

segs.p: “samaṇo khalu bho gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito icchānaṅgalaṁ anuppatto; icchānaṅgale viharati icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍe.
segs.e: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Icchānaṅgala. He is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala.

segs.p: Taṁ kho pana bhavantaṁ gotamaṁ evaṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato:
segs.e: He has this good reputation:

segs.p: ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi, satthā devamanussānaṁ buddho bhagavāti’.
segs.e: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’

segs.p: So imaṁ lokaṁ sadevakaṁ samārakaṁ sabrahmakaṁ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṁ pajaṁ sadevamanussaṁ sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti.
segs.e: He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others.

segs.p: So dhammaṁ deseti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāseti.
segs.e: He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: Sādhu kho pana tathārūpānaṁ arahataṁ dassanaṁ hotī”ti.
segs.e: It’s good to see such perfected ones.”

segs.p: Atha kho icchānaṅgalakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā tassā rattiyā accayena pahūtaṁ khādanīyaṁ bhojanīyaṁ ādāya yena icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bahidvārakoṭṭhake aṭṭhaṁsu uccāsaddamahāsaddā.
segs.e: Then, when the night had passed, they took abundant fresh and cooked foods and went to the forest near Icchānaṅgala, where they stood outside the gates making a colossal racket.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā nāgito bhagavato upaṭṭhāko hoti.
segs.e: Now, at that time Venerable Nāgita was the Buddha’s attendant.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṁ nāgitaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha said to Nāgita,

segs.p: “ke pana kho, nāgita, uccāsaddamahāsaddā, kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilope”ti?
segs.e: “Nāgita, who’s making that colossal racket? You’d think it was fishermen hauling in a catch!”

segs.p: “Ete, bhante, icchānaṅgalakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā pahūtaṁ khādanīyaṁ bhojanīyaṁ ādāya bahidvārakoṭṭhake ṭhitā bhagavantaññeva uddissa bhikkhusaṅghañcā”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, it’s these brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala. They’ve brought many fresh and cooked foods, and they’re standing outside the gates wanting to offer it specially to the Buddha and the mendicant Saṅgha.”

segs.p: “Māhaṁ, nāgita, yasena samāgamaṁ, mā ca mayā yaso.
segs.e: “Nāgita, may I never become famous. May fame not come to me.

segs.p: Yo kho, nāgita, nayimassa nekkhammasukhassa pavivekasukhassa upasamasukhassa sambodhasukhassa nikāmalābhī assa akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, yassāhaṁ nekkhammasukhassa pavivekasukhassa upasamasukhassa sambodhasukhassa nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī.
segs.e: There are those who can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

segs.p: So taṁ mīḷhasukhaṁ middhasukhaṁ lābhasakkārasilokasukhaṁ sādiyeyyā”ti.
segs.e: Let them enjoy the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honor, and popularity.”
“Sir, may the Blessed One please relent now! May the Holy One relent!
Now is the time for the Buddha to relent.

segs.p: Yena yeneva dāni bhagavā gamissati taṁninnāva gamissanti brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamā ceva jānapadā ca.
segs.e: Wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country will incline the same way.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhante, thullaphusitake deve vassante yathāninnaṁ udakāni pavattanti;
segs.e: It’s like when the heavens rain heavily and the water flows downhill.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhante, yena yeneva dāni bhagavā gamissati, taṁninnāva gamissanti brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamā ceva jānapadā ca.
segs.e: In the same way, wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders, and people of town and country will incline the same way.
Why is that?
Because of the Buddha’s ethics and wisdom.”

segs.p: “Māhaṁ, nāgita, yasena samāgamaṁ, mā ca mayā yaso.
segs.e: “Nāgita, may I never become famous. May fame not come to me.

segs.p: Yo kho, nāgita, nayimassa nekkhammasukhassa pavivekasukhassa upasamasukhassa sambodhasukhassa nikāmalābhī assa akicchalābhī akasiralābhī, yassāhaṁ nekkhammasukhassa pavivekasukhassa upasamasukhassa sambodhasukhassa nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī.
segs.e: There are those who can’t get the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of peace, the pleasure of awakening when they want, without trouble or difficulty like I can.

segs.p: So taṁ mīḷhasukhaṁ middhasukhaṁ lābhasakkārasilokasukhaṁ sādiyeyya.
segs.e: Let them enjoy the filthy, lazy pleasure of possessions, honor, and popularity.
What you eat, drink, chew, and taste ends up as excrement and urine.
This is its outcome.

segs.p: Piyānaṁ kho, nāgita, vipariṇāmaññathābhāvā uppajjanti sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā—
segs.e: When loved ones decay and perish, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
This is its outcome.

segs.p: Asubhanimittānuyogaṁ anuyuttassa kho, nāgita, subhanimitte pāṭikulyatā saṇṭhāti—
segs.e: When you pursue meditation on the feature of ugliness, revulsion at the feature of beauty becomes stabilized.
This is its outcome.

segs.p: Chasu kho, nāgita, phassāyatanesu aniccānupassino viharato phasse pāṭikulyatā saṇṭhāti—
segs.e: When you meditate observing impermanence in the six fields of contact, revulsion at contact becomes stabilized.
This is its outcome.

segs.p: Pañcasu kho, nāgita, upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassino viharato upādāne pāṭikulyatā saṇṭhāti—
segs.e: When you meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates, revulsion at grasping becomes stabilized.
This is its outcome.”
Numbered Discourses 5.31
4. With Sumanā
With Sumanā
At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho sumanā rājakumārī pañcahi rathasatehi pañcahi rājakumārisatehi parivutā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho sumanā rājakumārī bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Princess Sumanā, escorted by five hundred chariots and five hundred royal maidens, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “Idhassu, bhante, bhagavato dve sāvakā samasaddhā samasīlā samapaññā—
segs.e: “Sir, suppose there were two disciples equal in faith, ethics, and wisdom.
One is a giver, one is not.

segs.p: Te kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjeyyuṁ.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Devabhūtānaṁ pana nesaṁ, bhante, siyā viseso, siyā nānākaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: When they have become gods, would there be any distinction or difference between them?”
“There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “yo so, sumane, dāyako so amuṁ adāyakaṁ devabhūto samāno pañcahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhāti—
segs.e: “As a god, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in five respects:

segs.p: dibbena āyunā, dibbena vaṇṇena, dibbena sukhena, dibbena yasena, dibbena ādhipateyyena.
segs.e: heavenly lifespan, beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty.

segs.p: Yo so, sumane, dāyako so amuṁ adāyakaṁ devabhūto samāno imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhāti”.
segs.e: As a god, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in these five respects.”

segs.p: “Sace pana te, bhante, tato cutā itthattaṁ āgacchanti, manussabhūtānaṁ pana nesaṁ, bhante, siyā viseso, siyā nānākaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: “But sir, if they pass away from there and come back to this place as human beings, would there still be any distinction or difference between them?”
“There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “yo so, sumane, dāyako so amuṁ adāyakaṁ manussabhūto samāno pañcahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhāti—
segs.e: “As a human being, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in five respects:

segs.p: mānusakena āyunā, mānusakena vaṇṇena, mānusakena sukhena, mānusakena yasena, mānusakena ādhipateyyena.
segs.e: human lifespan, beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty.

segs.p: Yo so, sumane, dāyako so amuṁ adāyakaṁ manussabhūto samāno imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhāti”.
segs.e: As a human being, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in these five respects.”

segs.p: “Sace pana te, bhante, ubho agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajanti, pabbajitānaṁ pana nesaṁ, bhante, siyā viseso, siyā nānākaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: “But sir, if they both go forth from the lay life to homelessness, would there still be any distinction or difference between them?”
“There would be, Sumanā,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “yo so, sumane, dāyako so amuṁ adāyakaṁ pabbajito samāno pañcahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhāti—
segs.e: “As a renunciate, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in five respects.

segs.p: yācitova bahulaṁ cīvaraṁ paribhuñjati appaṁ ayācito, yācitova bahulaṁ piṇḍapātaṁ paribhuñjati appaṁ ayācito, yācitova bahulaṁ senāsanaṁ paribhuñjati appaṁ ayācito, yācitova bahulaṁ gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṁ paribhuñjati appaṁ ayācito.
segs.e: They usually use only what they’ve been invited to accept—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick—rarely using them without invitation.

segs.p: Yehi kho pana sabrahmacārīhi saddhiṁ viharati tyassa manāpeneva bahulaṁ kāyakammena samudācaranti appaṁ amanāpena, manāpeneva bahulaṁ vacīkammena samudācaranti appaṁ amanāpena, manāpeneva bahulaṁ manokammena samudācaranti appaṁ amanāpena, manāpaṁyeva bahulaṁ upahāraṁ upaharanti appaṁ amanāpaṁ.
segs.e: When living with other spiritual practitioners, they usually find themselves treated agreeably by them by way of body, speech, and mind, and rarely disagreeably. And they are usually presented with agreeable things by them, rarely with disagreeable ones.

segs.p: Yo so, sumane, dāyako so amuṁ adāyakaṁ pabbajito samāno imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhātī”ti.
segs.e: As a renunciate, the one who was a giver surpasses the other in these five respects.”

segs.p: “Sace pana te, bhante, ubho arahattaṁ pāpuṇanti, arahattappattānaṁ pana nesaṁ, bhante, siyā viseso, siyā nānākaraṇan”ti?
segs.e: “But sir, if they both attain perfection, as perfected ones would there still be any distinction or difference between them?”

segs.p: “Ettha kho panesāhaṁ, sumane, na kiñci nānākaraṇaṁ vadāmi, yadidaṁ vimuttiyā vimuttin”ti.
segs.e: “In that case, I say there is no difference between the freedom of one and the freedom of the other.”
“It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing!

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhante, alameva dānāni dātuṁ alaṁ puññāni kātuṁ;
segs.e: This is quite enough to justify giving gifts and making merit.

segs.p: yatra hi nāma devabhūtassāpi upakārāni puññāni, manussabhūtassāpi upakārāni puññāni, pabbajitassāpi upakārāni puññānī”ti.
segs.e: For merit is helpful for those who have become gods, human beings, and renunciates.”
“That’s so true, Sumanā.

segs.p: Alañhi, sumane, dānāni dātuṁ alaṁ puññāni kātuṁ.
segs.e: It’s quite enough to justify giving gifts and making merit.

segs.p: Devabhūtassāpi upakārāni puññāni, manussabhūtassāpi upakārāni puññāni, pabbajitassāpi upakārāni puññānī”ti.
segs.e: For merit is helpful for those who have become gods, human beings, and renunciates.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“The moon so immaculate,
journeying across the dimension of space;
outshines with its radiance
all the world’s stars.
So too, a faithful individual,
perfect in ethics,
outshines with their generosity
all the world’s stingy people.
The thundering rain cloud,
its hundred peaks wreathed in lightning,
pours down over the rich earth,
soaking the uplands and valleys.
Even so, an astute person accomplished in vision,
a disciple of the fully awakened Buddha,
surpasses a stingy person
in five respects:
long life and fame,
beauty and happiness.
Lavished with riches,
they depart to rejoice in heaven.”
Numbered Discourses 5.32
4. With Sumanā
With Cundī

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

segs.p: Atha kho cundī rājakumārī pañcahi rathasatehi pañcahi ca kumārisatehi parivutā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho cundī rājakumārī bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Princess Cundī, escorted by five hundred chariots and five hundred royal maidens, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “Amhākaṁ, bhante, bhātā cundo nāma rājakumāro, so evamāha:
segs.e: “Sir, my brother, Prince Cunda, says this:

segs.p: ‘yadeva so hoti itthī vā puriso vā buddhaṁ saraṇaṁ gato, dhammaṁ saraṇaṁ gato, saṅghaṁ saraṇaṁ gato, pāṇātipātā paṭivirato, adinnādānā paṭivirato, kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato, musāvādā paṭivirato, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato, so kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁyeva upapajjati, no duggatin’ti.
segs.e: ‘Take a woman or man who goes for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha, and doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor. Only then do they get reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when their body breaks up, after death.’
And so I ask the Buddha:

segs.p: ‘kathaṁrūpe kho, bhante, satthari pasanno kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁyeva upapajjati, no duggatiṁ?
segs.e: Sir, what kind of teacher should you have confidence in so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?

segs.p: Kathaṁrūpe dhamme pasanno kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁyeva upapajjati, no duggatiṁ?
segs.e: Sir, what kind of teaching should you have confidence in so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?

segs.p: Kathaṁrūpe saṅghe pasanno kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁyeva upapajjati, no duggatiṁ?
segs.e: Sir, what kind of Saṅgha should you have confidence in so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?

segs.p: Kathaṁrūpesu sīlesu paripūrakārī kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁyeva upapajjati, no duggatin’”ti?
segs.e: Sir, what kind of ethics should you fulfill so as to be reborn in a good place, not a bad place, when the body breaks up, after death?”

segs.p: “Yāvatā, cundi, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā catuppadā vā bahuppadā vā rūpino vā arūpino vā saññino vā asaññino vā nevasaññināsaññino vā, tathāgato tesaṁ aggamakkhāyati arahaṁ sammāsambuddho.
segs.e: “Cundī, the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is said to be the best of all sentient beings—be they footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; with perception or without perception or with neither perception nor non-perception.

segs.p: Ye kho, cundi, buddhe pasannā, agge te pasannā.
segs.e: Those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the best.

segs.p: Agge kho pana pasannānaṁ aggo vipāko hoti.
segs.e: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

segs.p: Yāvatā, cundi, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṁ aggamakkhāyati.
segs.e: The noble eightfold path is said to be the best of all conditioned things.

segs.p: Ye, cundi, ariye aṭṭhaṅgike magge pasannā, agge te pasannā, agge kho pana pasannānaṁ aggo vipāko hoti.
segs.e: Those who have confidence in the noble eightfold path have confidence in the best. Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

segs.p: Yāvatā, cundi, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṁ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṁ—
segs.e: Fading away is said to be the best of all things whether conditioned or unconditioned.

segs.p: madanimmadano pipāsavinayo ālayasamugghāto vaṭṭupacchedo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbānaṁ.
segs.e: That is, the quelling of vanity, the removing of thirst, the uprooting of clinging, the breaking of the round, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.

segs.p: Ye kho, cundi, virāge dhamme pasannā, agge te pasannā.
segs.e: Those who have confidence in the teaching of fading away have confidence in the best.

segs.p: Agge kho pana pasannānaṁ aggo vipāko hoti.
segs.e: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

segs.p: Yāvatā, cundi, saṅghā vā gaṇā vā, tathāgatasāvakasaṅgho tesaṁ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṁ—
segs.e: The Saṅgha of the Realized One’s disciples is said to be the best of all communities and groups.

segs.p: cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṁ puññakkhettaṁ lokassa.
segs.e: It consists of the four pairs, the eight individual persons. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with cupped palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.

segs.p: Ye kho, cundi, saṅghe pasannā, agge te pasannā.
segs.e: Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the best.

segs.p: Agge kho pana pasannānaṁ aggo vipāko hoti.
segs.e: Having confidence in the best, the result is the best.

segs.p: Yāvatā, cundi, sīlāni, ariyakantāni sīlāni tesaṁ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṁ—
segs.e: The ethical conduct loved by the noble ones is said to be the best of all ethics.

segs.p: akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṁvattanikāni.
segs.e: It is intact, impeccable, spotless, and unmarred, liberating, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion.

segs.p: Ye kho, cundi, ariyakantesu sīlesu paripūrakārino, agge te paripūrakārino.
segs.e: Those who fulfill the ethics loved by the noble ones fulfill the best.

segs.p: Agge kho pana paripūrakārīnaṁ aggo vipāko hotīti.
segs.e: Fulfilling the best, the result is the best.
For those who, knowing the best teaching,
base their confidence on the best—
confident in the best Awakened One,
supremely worthy of a religious donation;
confident in the best teaching,
the bliss of fading and stilling;
confident in the best Saṅgha,
the supreme field of merit—
giving gifts to the best,
the best of merit grows:
the best lifespan, beauty,
fame, reputation, happiness, and strength.
An intelligent person gives to the best,
settled on the best teaching.
When they become a god or human,
they rejoice at reaching the best.”
Numbered Discourses 5.33
4. With Sumanā
With Uggaha

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā bhaddiye viharati jātiyā vane.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Bhaddiya in Jātiyā Wood.

segs.p: Atha kho uggaho meṇḍakanattā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho uggaho meṇḍakanattā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Uggaha, Meṇḍaka’s grandson, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “Adhivāsetu me, bhante, bhagavā svātanāya attacatuttho bhattan”ti.
segs.e: “Sir, would the Buddha, together with three other monks, please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?”
The Buddha consented with silence.

segs.p: Atha kho uggaho meṇḍakanattā bhagavato adhivāsanaṁ viditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā pakkāmi.
segs.e: Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Uggaha rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on his right, before leaving.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena uggahassa meṇḍakanattuno nivesanaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then when the night had passed, the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to Uggaha’s home, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

segs.p: Atha kho uggaho meṇḍakanattā bhagavantaṁ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi.
segs.e: Then Uggaha served and satisfied the Buddha with his own hands with delicious fresh and cooked foods.

segs.p: Atha kho uggaho meṇḍakanattā bhagavantaṁ bhuttāviṁ onītapattapāṇiṁ ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: When the Buddha had eaten and washed his hand and bowl, Uggaha sat down to one side,

segs.p: Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho uggaho meṇḍakanattā bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: and said to him,
“Sir, these girls of mine will be going to their husbands’ families.
May the Buddha please advise

segs.p: anusāsatu tāsaṁ, bhante, bhagavā, yaṁ tāsaṁ assa dīgharattaṁ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.
segs.e: and instruct them. It will be for their lasting welfare and happiness.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā tā kumāriyo etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the Buddha said to those girls:
“So, girls, you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘yassa vo mātāpitaro bhattuno dassanti atthakāmā hitesino anukampakā anukampaṁ upādāya, tassa bhavissāma pubbuṭṭhāyiniyo pacchānipātiniyo kiṅkārapaṭissāviniyo manāpacāriniyo piyavādiniyo’ti.
segs.e: ‘Our parents will give us to a husband wanting what’s best, out of kindness and sympathy. We will get up before him and go to bed after him, and be obliging, behaving nicely and speaking politely.’
That’s how you should train.
So, girls, you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘ye te bhattu garuno bhavissanti mātāti vā pitāti vā samaṇabrāhmaṇāti vā, te sakkarissāma garuṁ karissāma mānessāma pūjessāma abbhāgate ca āsanodakena paṭipūjessāmā’ti.
segs.e: ‘Those our husband respects—mother and father, ascetics and brahmins—we will honor, respect, revere, and venerate, and serve with a seat and a drink when they come as guests.’
That’s how you should train.
So, girls, you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘ye te bhattu abbhantarā kammantā uṇṇāti vā kappāsāti vā, tattha dakkhā bhavissāma analasā, tatrupāyāya vīmaṁsāya samannāgatā, alaṁ kātuṁ alaṁ saṁvidhātun’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will be deft and tireless in doing domestic duties for our husband, such as knitting and sewing. We will have an understanding of how to go about things in order to complete and organize the work.’
That’s how you should train.
So, girls, you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘yo so bhattu abbhantaro antojano dāsāti vā pessāti vā kammakarāti vā, tesaṁ katañca katato jānissāma akatañca akatato jānissāma, gilānakānañca balābalaṁ jānissāma, khādanīyaṁ bhojanīyañcassa paccaṁsena saṁvibhajissāmā’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will know what work our husband’s domestic bondservants, servants, and workers have completed, and what they’ve left incomplete. We will know who is sick, and who is fit or unwell. We will distribute to each a fair portion of fresh and cooked foods.’
That’s how you should train.
So, girls, you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘yaṁ bhattā āharissati dhanaṁ vā dhaññaṁ vā rajataṁ vā jātarūpaṁ vā, taṁ ārakkhena guttiyā sampādessāma, tattha ca bhavissāma adhuttī athenī asoṇḍī avināsikāyo’ti.
segs.e: ‘We will ensure that any income our husbands earn is guarded and protected, whether money, grain, silver, or gold. We will not overspend, steal, waste, or lose it.’
That’s how you should train.

segs.p: Imehi kho, kumāriyo, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā manāpakāyikānaṁ devānaṁ sahabyataṁ upapajjatīti.
segs.e: When they possess these five qualities, ladies—when their body breaks up, after death—are reborn in company with the Gods of the Agreeable Host.
She’d never look down on her husband,
who’s always eager to work hard,
always looking after her,
and bringing whatever she wants.
And a good woman never scolds her husband
with jealous words.
Being astute, she reveres
those respected by her husband.
She gets up early, works tirelessly,
and manages the domestic help.
She’s agreeable to her husband,
and preserves his wealth.
A lady who fulfills these duties
according to her husband’s desire,
is reborn among the gods
called ‘Agreeable’.”
Numbered Discourses 5.34
4. With Sumanā
With General Sīha

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Atha kho sīho senāpati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho sīho senāpati bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then General Sīha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and asked him,

segs.p: “sakkā nu kho, bhante, bhagavā sandiṭṭhikaṁ dānaphalaṁ paññāpetun”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, can you point out a fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life?”
“I can, Sīha,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “dāyako, sīha, dānapati bahuno janassa piyo hoti manāpo.
segs.e: “A giver, a donor is dear and beloved to many people.

segs.p: Yampi, sīha, dāyako dānapati bahuno janassa piyo hoti manāpo, idampi sandiṭṭhikaṁ dānaphalaṁ.
segs.e: This is a fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, sīha, dāyakaṁ dānapatiṁ santo sappurisā bhajanti.
segs.e: Furthermore, good and true persons associate with a giver.

segs.p: Yampi, sīha, dāyakaṁ dānapatiṁ santo sappurisā bhajanti, idampi sandiṭṭhikaṁ dānaphalaṁ.
segs.e: This is another fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, sīha, dāyakassa dānapatino kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchati.
segs.e: Furthermore, a giver gains a good reputation.

segs.p: Yampi, sīha, dāyakassa dānapatino kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, idampi sandiṭṭhikaṁ dānaphalaṁ.
segs.e: This is another fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, sīha, dāyako dānapati yaṁ yadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkamati—yadi khattiyaparisaṁ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṁ yadi gahapatiparisaṁ yadi samaṇaparisaṁ—visārado upasaṅkamati amaṅkubhūto.
segs.e: Furthermore, a giver enters any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

segs.p: Yampi, sīha, dāyako dānapati yaṁ yadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkamati—yadi khattiyaparisaṁ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṁ yadi gahapatiparisaṁ yadi samaṇaparisaṁ—visārado upasaṅkamati amaṅkubhūto, idampi sandiṭṭhikaṁ dānaphalaṁ.
segs.e: This is another fruit of giving that’s apparent in the present life.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, sīha, dāyako dānapati kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: Furthermore, when a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Yampi, sīha, dāyako dānapati kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjati, idaṁ samparāyikaṁ dānaphalan”ti.
segs.e: This is a fruit of giving to do with lives to come.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, sīho senāpati bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, General Sīha said to the Buddha,

segs.p: “yānimāni, bhante, bhagavatā cattāri sandiṭṭhikāni dānaphalāni akkhātāni, nāhaṁ ettha bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmi; ahaṁ petāni jānāmi.
segs.e: “When it comes to those four fruits of giving that are apparent in the present life, I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha, for I know them too.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati bahuno janassa piyo manāpo.
segs.e: I’m a giver, a donor, and am dear and beloved to many people.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati; maṁ santo sappurisā bhajanti.
segs.e: I’m a giver, and good and true persons associate with me.

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati; mayhaṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato: ‘sīho senāpati dāyako kārako saṅghupaṭṭhāko’ti.
segs.e: I’m a giver, and I have this good reputation: ‘General Sīha gives, serves, and attends on the Saṅgha.’

segs.p: Ahaṁ, bhante, dāyako dānapati yaṁ yadeva parisaṁ upasaṅkamāmi—yadi khattiyaparisaṁ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṁ yadi gahapatiparisaṁ yadi samaṇaparisaṁ—visārado upasaṅkamāmi amaṅkubhūto.
segs.e: I’m a giver, and I enter any kind of assembly bold and self-assured, whether it’s an assembly of aristocrats, brahmins, householders, or ascetics.

segs.p: Yānimāni, bhante, bhagavatā cattāri sandiṭṭhikāni dānaphalāni akkhātāni, nāhaṁ ettha bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmi; ahaṁ petāni jānāmi.
segs.e: When it comes to these four fruits of giving that are apparent in the present life, I don’t rely on faith in the Buddha, for I know them too.

segs.p: Yañca kho maṁ, bhante, bhagavā evamāha:
segs.e: But when the Buddha says:

segs.p: ‘dāyako, sīha, dānapati kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjatī’ti, etāhaṁ na jānāmi; ettha ca panāhaṁ bhagavato saddhāya gacchāmī”ti.
segs.e: ‘When a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.’ I don’t know this, so I have to rely on faith in the Buddha.”
“That’s so true, Sīha! That’s so true!

segs.p: Dāyako dānapati kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjatīti.
segs.e: When a giver’s body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Dadaṁ piyo hoti bhajanti naṁ bahū,
segs.e: Giving, you’re loved and befriended by many people.
You get a good reputation, and your fame grows.
A generous man enters an assembly
bold and self-assured.
So an astute person, seeking happiness, <j>would give gifts,
having driven out the stain of stinginess.
They live long in the Third Heaven,
enjoying the company of the gods.
Having taken the opportunity to do good, <j>when they pass from here
they wander self-radiant in the Garden of Delight.
There they delight, rejoice, and enjoy themselves,
provided with the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
Having practiced the word of the unattached, <j>the unaffected,
disciples of the Holy One rejoice in heaven.”
Numbered Discourses 5.35
4. With Sumanā
The Benefits of Giving
“Mendicants, there are five benefits of giving.
What five?
A giver, a donor is dear and beloved by many people.
Good and true persons associate with them.
They get a good reputation.
They don’t neglect a layperson’s duties.

segs.p: kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca dāne ānisaṁsāti.
segs.e: These are the five benefits of giving.
Giving, one is loved,
and follows the way of the good.
The good, disciplined spiritual practitioners
always associate with you.
They teach you the Dhamma
that casts aside all suffering.
Having understood this teaching,
the undefiled one is fully extinguished.”
Numbered Discourses 5.36
4. With Sumanā
Timely Gifts
“Mendicants, there are these five timely gifts.
What five?
A gift to a visitor.
A gift to someone setting out on a journey.
A gift to someone who is sick.
A gift at a time of famine.

segs.p: yāni tāni navasassāni navaphalāni tāni paṭhamaṁ sīlavantesu patiṭṭhāpeti.
segs.e: Presenting the freshly harvested grains and fruits first to those who are ethical.
These are the five timely gifts.
The wise give at the right time,
being bountiful and rid of stinginess.
A religious donation at the right time
to the noble ones, upright and unaffected,
given with a clear and confident mind,
is indeed abundant.
Those who rejoice at that,
or do other services,
don’t miss out on the offering;
they too have a share in the merit.
So you should give without holding back,
where a gift is very fruitful.
The good deeds of sentient beings
support them in the next world.”
Numbered Discourses 5.37
4. With Sumanā
Food

segs.p: “Bhojanaṁ, bhikkhave, dadamāno dāyako paṭiggāhakānaṁ pañca ṭhānāni deti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, when a giver gives food, they give the recipients five things.
What five?

segs.p: Āyuṁ deti, vaṇṇaṁ deti, sukhaṁ deti, balaṁ deti, paṭibhānaṁ deti.
segs.e: Long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and eloquence.

segs.p: Āyuṁ kho pana datvā āyussa bhāgī hoti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā;
segs.e: Giving long life, they have long life as a god or human.

segs.p: vaṇṇaṁ datvā vaṇṇassa bhāgī hoti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā;
segs.e: Giving beauty, they have beauty as a god or human.

segs.p: sukhaṁ datvā sukhassa bhāgī hoti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā;
segs.e: Giving happiness, they have happiness as a god or human.

segs.p: balaṁ datvā balassa bhāgī hoti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā;
segs.e: Giving strength, they have strength as a god or human.

segs.p: paṭibhānaṁ datvā paṭibhānassa bhāgī hoti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā.
segs.e: Giving eloquence, they are eloquent as a god or human.

segs.p: Bhojanaṁ, bhikkhave, dadamāno dāyako paṭiggāhakānaṁ imāni pañca ṭhānāni detīti.
segs.e: When a giver gives food, they give the recipients five things.
Being attentive, one is a giver of life, strength,
beauty, and eloquence.
An intelligent giver of happiness
gains happiness in return.
Giving life, strength, beauty,
happiness, and eloquence,
they’re long-lived and famous
wherever they’re reborn.”
Numbered Discourses 5.38
4. With Sumanā
Faith
“Mendicants, a faithful gentleman gets five benefits.
What five?

segs.p: Ye te, bhikkhave, loke santo sappurisā te saddhaññeva paṭhamaṁ anukampantā anukampanti, no tathā assaddhaṁ;
segs.e: The true persons in the world show sympathy first to the faithful, not so much to the unfaithful.

segs.p: saddhaññeva paṭhamaṁ upasaṅkamantā upasaṅkamanti, no tathā assaddhaṁ;
segs.e: They first approach the faithful, not so much the unfaithful.

segs.p: saddhaññeva paṭhamaṁ paṭiggaṇhantā paṭiggaṇhanti, no tathā assaddhaṁ;
segs.e: They first receive alms from the faithful, not so much the unfaithful.

segs.p: saddhaññeva paṭhamaṁ dhammaṁ desentā desenti, no tathā assaddhaṁ;
segs.e: They first teach Dhamma to the faithful, not so much the unfaithful.

segs.p: saddho kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā sugatiṁ saggaṁ lokaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, the faithful are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca saddhe kulaputte ānisaṁsā.
segs.e: A faithful gentleman gets these five benefits.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, subhūmiyaṁ catumahāpathe mahānigrodho samantā pakkhīnaṁ paṭisaraṇaṁ hoti;
segs.e: Suppose there was a great banyan tree at a level crossroads. It would become a refuge for birds from all around.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, saddho kulaputto bahuno janassa paṭisaraṇaṁ hoti bhikkhūnaṁ bhikkhunīnaṁ upāsakānaṁ upāsikānanti.
segs.e: In the same way, a faithful gentleman becomes a refuge for many people—monks, nuns, laywomen, and laymen.
With its branches, leaves, and fruit,
a great tree with its strong trunk,
firmly-rooted and fruit-bearing,
supports many birds.
It’s a lovely place,
frequented by the sky-soarers.
Those that need shade go in the shade,
those that need fruit enjoy the fruit.
So too, a faithful individual
is perfect in ethics,
placid in manner and amenable,
gentle, courteous, and tender.
Those free of greed, freed of hate,
free of delusion, undefiled,
fields of merit for the world,
associate with such a person.
They teach them the Dhamma,
that casts aside all suffering.
Having understood this teaching,
the undefiled one is fully extinguished.”
Numbered Discourses 5.39
4. With Sumanā
A Child

segs.p: “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, ṭhānāni sampassantā mātāpitaro puttaṁ icchanti kule jāyamānaṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, parents see five reasons to wish for the birth of a child in the family.
What five?
Since we looked after them, they’ll look after us.
They’ll do their duty for us.
The family customs will last.
They’ll take care of the inheritance.

segs.p: atha vā pana petānaṁ kālaṅkatānaṁ dakkhiṇaṁ anuppadassatīti.
segs.e: Or else when we have passed away they’ll give an offering on our behalf.

segs.p: Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca ṭhānāni sampassantā mātāpitaro puttaṁ icchanti kule jāyamānanti.
segs.e: Parents see these five reasons to wish for the birth of a child in the family.
Seeing five reasons,
astute people wish for a child.
Since we looked after them, they’ll look after us.
They’ll do their duty for us.
The family customs will last.
They’ll take care of the inheritance.
Or else when we have passed away
they’ll give an offering on our behalf.
Seeing these five reasons
astute people wish for a child.
And so true persons,
grateful and thankful,
look after their parents,
remembering past deeds.
They do for their parents,
as their parents did for them in the past.
Following their advice, <j>looking after those who raised them,
the family customs are not lost.
Faithful, accomplished in ethics,
such a child is praiseworthy.”
Numbered Discourses 5.40
4. With Sumanā
Great Sal Trees

segs.p: “Himavantaṁ, bhikkhave, pabbatarājaṁ nissāya mahāsālā pañcahi vaḍḍhīhi vaḍḍhanti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, great sal trees grow in five ways supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.
What five?
The branches, leaves, and foliage;
the bark;
the shoots;
the softwood;
and the hardwood.

segs.p: Himavantaṁ, bhikkhave, pabbatarājaṁ nissāya mahāsālā imāhi pañcahi vaḍḍhīhi vaḍḍhanti.
segs.e: Great sal trees grow in these five ways supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, saddhaṁ kulaputtaṁ nissāya antojano pañcahi vaḍḍhīhi vaḍḍhati.
segs.e: In the same way, a family grows in five ways supported by a family head with faith.
What five?
Faith,
ethics,
learning,
generosity,
and wisdom.

segs.p: Saddhaṁ, bhikkhave, kulaputtaṁ nissāya antojano imāhi pañcahi vaḍḍhīhi vaḍḍhatīti.
segs.e: A family grows in these five ways supported by a family head with faith.
Supported by the rocky mountain
in the wilds, the formidable forest,
the tree grows
to become lord of the forest.
So too, when the family head
is ethical and faithful,
supported by them, they grow:
children, partners, and kin,
colleagues, relatives,
and those dependent for their livelihood.
Seeing the ethical conduct of the virtuous,
the generosity and good deeds,
those who see clearly
do likewise.
Having practiced the teaching here,
the path that goes to a good place,
they delight in the heavenly realm,
enjoying all the pleasures they desire.”
Numbered Discourses 5.41
5. With King Muṇḍa
Getting Rich

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho anāthapiṇḍikaṁ gahapatiṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:
“Householder, there are these five reasons to get rich.
What five?

segs.p: Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi bhogehi bāhābalaparicitehi sedāvakkhittehi dhammikehi dhammaladdhehi attānaṁ sukheti pīṇeti sammā sukhaṁ pariharati;
segs.e: Firstly, with his legitimate wealth—earned by his efforts and initiative, built up with his own hands, gathered by the sweat of the brow—a noble disciple makes himself happy and pleased, keeping himself properly happy.

segs.p: mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti sammā sukhaṁ pariharati;
segs.e: He makes his mother and father happy …

segs.p: puttadāradāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti sammā sukhaṁ pariharati.
segs.e: He makes his children, partners, bondservants, workers, and staff happy …
This is the first reason to get rich.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, gahapati, ariyasāvako uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi bhogehi bāhābalaparicitehi sedāvakkhittehi dhammikehi dhammaladdhehi mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti sammā sukhaṁ pariharati.
segs.e: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he makes his friends and colleagues happy …
This is the second reason to get rich.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, gahapati, ariyasāvako uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi bhogehi bāhābalaparicitehi sedāvakkhittehi dhammikehi dhammaladdhehi yā tā honti āpadā—
segs.e: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he protects himself against losses from such things as fire, water, kings, bandits, or unloved heirs.

segs.p: aggito vā udakato vā rājato vā corato vā appiyato vā dāyādato—
tathārūpāsu āpadāsu bhogehi pariyodhāya vattati, sotthiṁ attānaṁ karoti.
segs.e: He keeps himself safe.
This is the third reason to get rich.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, gahapati, ariyasāvako uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi bhogehi bāhābalaparicitehi sedāvakkhittehi dhammikehi dhammaladdhehi pañcabaliṁ kattā hoti.
segs.e: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he makes five spirit-offerings:
to relatives, guests, ancestors, king, and deities.
This is the fourth reason to get rich.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, gahapati, ariyasāvako uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatehi bhogehi bāhābalaparicitehi sedāvakkhittehi dhammikehi dhammaladdhehi ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā madappamādā paṭiviratā khantisoracce niviṭṭhā ekamattānaṁ damenti ekamattānaṁ samenti ekamattānaṁ parinibbāpenti, tathārūpesu samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṁ dakkhiṇaṁ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṁ sukhavipākaṁ saggasaṁvattanikaṁ.
segs.e: Furthermore, with his legitimate wealth he establishes an uplifting religious donation for ascetics and brahmins—those who refrain from intoxication and negligence, are settled in patience and gentleness, and who tame, calm, and extinguish themselves—that’s conducive to heaven, ripens in happiness, and leads to heaven.
This is the fifth reason to get rich.

segs.p: Ime kho, gahapati, pañca bhogānaṁ ādiyā.
segs.e: These are the five reasons to get rich.

segs.p: Tassa ce, gahapati, ariyasāvakassa ime pañca bhogānaṁ ādiye ādiyato bhogā parikkhayaṁ gacchanti, tassa evaṁ hoti:
segs.e: Now if the riches a noble disciple gets for these five reasons run out, he thinks:

segs.p: ‘ye vata bhogānaṁ ādiyā te cāhaṁ ādiyāmi bhogā ca me parikkhayaṁ gacchantī’ti.
segs.e: ‘So, the riches I have obtained for these reasons are running out.’
And so he has no regrets.

segs.p: Tassa ce, gahapati, ariyasāvakassa ime pañca bhogānaṁ ādiye ādiyato bhogā abhivaḍḍhanti, tassa evaṁ hoti:
segs.e: But if the riches a noble disciple gets for these five reasons increase, he thinks:

segs.p: ‘ye vata bhogānaṁ ādiyā te cāhaṁ ādiyāmi bhogā ca me abhivaḍḍhantī’ti.
segs.e: ‘So, the riches I have obtained for these reasons are increasing.’
And so he has no regrets in both cases.
‘I’ve enjoyed my wealth, <j>supporting those who depend on me;
I’ve overcome losses;
I’ve given uplifting religious donations;
and made the five spirit-offerings.
I have looked after the ethical and
disciplined spiritual practitioners.
I’ve achieved the goal
for which an astute layperson
wishes to gain wealth.
I don’t regret what I’ve done.’
A mortal man who recollects this
stands firm in the teaching of the noble ones.
They’re praised in this life by the astute,
and they depart to rejoice in heaven.”
Numbered Discourses 5.42
5. With King Muṇḍa
A True Person

segs.p: “Sappuriso, bhikkhave, kule jāyamāno bahuno janassa atthāya hitāya sukhāya hoti;
segs.e: “Mendicants, a true person is born in a family for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the people.
For the benefit, welfare, and happiness of mother and father;
children and partners;
bondservants, workers, and staff;
friends and colleagues;
and ascetics and brahmins.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāmegho sabbasassāni sampādento bahuno janassa atthāya hitāya sukhāya hoti;
segs.e: It’s like a great rain cloud, which nourishes all the crops for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the people.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, sappuriso kule jāyamāno bahuno janassa atthāya hitāya sukhāya hoti;
segs.e: In the same way, a true person is born in a family for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the people. …
The gods protect one who is guarded by principle,
who uses their wealth for the welfare of the many.
One who is learned, <j>with precepts and observances intact,
and steady in principle, doesn’t lose their reputation.
Firm in principle, accomplished in ethical conduct,
truthful, conscientious;
like a pendant of Black Plum River gold,
who is worthy to criticize them?
Even the gods praise them,
and by the Divinity, too, they’re praised.”
Numbered Discourses 5.43
5. With King Muṇḍa
Likable

segs.p: Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho anāthapiṇḍikaṁ gahapatiṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:

segs.p: “Pañcime, gahapati, dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dullabhā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: “Householder, these five things, which are likable, desirable, and agreeable are hard to get in the world.
What five?

segs.p: Āyu, gahapati, iṭṭho kanto manāpo dullabho lokasmiṁ;
segs.e: Long life,

segs.p: vaṇṇo iṭṭho kanto manāpo dullabho lokasmiṁ;
segs.e: beauty,

segs.p: sukhaṁ iṭṭhaṁ kantaṁ manāpaṁ dullabhaṁ lokasmiṁ;
segs.e: happiness,

segs.p: yaso iṭṭho kanto manāpo dullabho lokasmiṁ;
segs.e: fame,

segs.p: saggā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dullabhā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: and heaven.

segs.p: Ime kho, gahapati, pañca dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā dullabhā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: These are the five things, which are likable, desirable, and agreeable, but hard to get in the world.

segs.p: Imesaṁ kho, gahapati, pañcannaṁ dhammānaṁ iṭṭhānaṁ kantānaṁ manāpānaṁ dullabhānaṁ lokasmiṁ na āyācanahetu vā patthanāhetu vā paṭilābhaṁ vadāmi.
segs.e: And I say that these five things are not got by supplication or wishing for them.

segs.p: Imesaṁ kho, gahapati, pañcannaṁ dhammānaṁ iṭṭhānaṁ kantānaṁ manāpānaṁ dullabhānaṁ lokasmiṁ āyācanahetu vā patthanāhetu vā paṭilābho abhavissa, ko idha kena hāyetha?
segs.e: If they were, who would lack them?

segs.p: Na kho, gahapati, arahati ariyasāvako āyukāmo āyuṁ āyācituṁ vā abhinandituṁ vā āyussa vāpi hetu.
segs.e: A noble disciple who wants to live long ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

segs.p: Āyukāmena, gahapati, ariyasāvakena āyusaṁvattanikā paṭipadā paṭipajjitabbā.
segs.e: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to long life.

segs.p: Āyusaṁvattanikā hissa paṭipadā paṭipannā āyupaṭilābhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: For by practicing that way they gain long life

segs.p: So lābhī hoti āyussa dibbassa vā mānusassa vā.
segs.e: as a god or a human being.

segs.p: Na kho, gahapati, arahati ariyasāvako vaṇṇakāmo vaṇṇaṁ āyācituṁ vā abhinandituṁ vā vaṇṇassa vāpi hetu.
segs.e: A noble disciple who wants to be beautiful ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

segs.p: Vaṇṇakāmena, gahapati, ariyasāvakena vaṇṇasaṁvattanikā paṭipadā paṭipajjitabbā.
segs.e: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to beauty.

segs.p: Vaṇṇasaṁvattanikā hissa paṭipadā paṭipannā vaṇṇapaṭilābhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: For by practicing that way they gain beauty

segs.p: So lābhī hoti vaṇṇassa dibbassa vā mānusassa vā.
segs.e: as a god or a human being.

segs.p: Na kho, gahapati, arahati ariyasāvako sukhakāmo sukhaṁ āyācituṁ vā abhinandituṁ vā sukhassa vāpi hetu.
segs.e: A noble disciple who wants to be happy ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

segs.p: Sukhakāmena, gahapati, ariyasāvakena sukhasaṁvattanikā paṭipadā paṭipajjitabbā.
segs.e: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to happiness.

segs.p: Sukhasaṁvattanikā hissa paṭipadā paṭipannā sukhapaṭilābhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: For by practicing that way they gain happiness

segs.p: So lābhī hoti sukhassa dibbassa vā mānusassa vā.
segs.e: as a god or a human being.

segs.p: Na kho, gahapati, arahati ariyasāvako yasakāmo yasaṁ āyācituṁ vā abhinandituṁ vā yasassa vāpi hetu.
segs.e: A noble disciple who wants to be famous ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

segs.p: Yasakāmena, gahapati, ariyasāvakena yasasaṁvattanikā paṭipadā paṭipajjitabbā.
segs.e: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to fame.

segs.p: Yasasaṁvattanikā hissa paṭipadā paṭipannā yasapaṭilābhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: For by practicing that way they gain fame

segs.p: So lābhī hoti yasassa dibbassa vā mānusassa vā.
segs.e: as a god or a human being.

segs.p: Na kho, gahapati, arahati ariyasāvako saggakāmo saggaṁ āyācituṁ vā abhinandituṁ vā saggānaṁ vāpi hetu.
segs.e: A noble disciple who wants to go to heaven ought not pray for it, or hope for it, or pine for it.

segs.p: Saggakāmena, gahapati, ariyasāvakena saggasaṁvattanikā paṭipadā paṭipajjitabbā.
segs.e: Instead, they should practice the way that leads to heaven.

segs.p: Saggasaṁvattanikā hissa paṭipadā paṭipannā saggapaṭilābhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: For by practicing that way they gain heaven,
they are one who gains the heavens.
For one who desires lofty delights
again and again—
long life, beauty, fame and reputation,
heaven, and an eminent family—
the astute praise diligence
in making merit.
Being diligent, an astute person
secures both benefits:
the benefit in this life,
and in lives to come.
An attentive one, comprehending the meaning,
is said to be astute.”
Numbered Discourses 5.44
5. With King Muṇḍa
Agreeable

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena uggassa gahapatino vesālikassa nivesanaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.
segs.e: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the householder Ugga of Vesālī, where he sat down on the seat spread out.

segs.p: Atha kho uggo gahapati vesāliko yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho uggo gahapati vesāliko bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Ugga went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, bhante, bhagavato sutaṁ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ:
segs.e: “Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:
‘The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable.’
My sal flower porridge is agreeable:

segs.p: taṁ me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: may the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”
So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, bhante, bhagavato sutaṁ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ:
segs.e: “Sir, I have heard and learned this in the presence of the Buddha:
‘The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable.’
My pork with jujube is agreeable:

segs.p: taṁ me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: may the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”
So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, bhante, bhagavato sutaṁ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ:

segs.e: “… My fried vegetable stalks are agreeable:

segs.p: taṁ me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: may the Buddha please accept them from me out of sympathy.”
So the Buddha accepted them out of sympathy.

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, bhante, bhagavato sutaṁ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ:
Manāpo me, bhante, sālīnaṁ odano vicitakāḷako anekasūpo anekabyañjano;
segs.e: “… My boiled fine rice with the dark grains picked out, served with many soups and sauces is agreeable:

segs.p: taṁ me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: may the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”
So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, bhante, bhagavato sutaṁ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ:

segs.e: “… My cloths imported from Kāsi are agreeable:

segs.p: tāni me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: may the Buddha please accept them from me out of sympathy.”
So the Buddha accepted them out of sympathy.

segs.p: “Sammukhā metaṁ, bhante, bhagavato sutaṁ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṁ:
Manāpo me, bhante, pallaṅko gonakatthato paṭalikatthato kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo sauttaracchado ubhatolohitakūpadhāno.
segs.e: “… My couch spread with woolen covers—shag-piled or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends is agreeable.
But, sir, I know that
this is not proper for the Buddha.

segs.p: Idaṁ me, bhante, candanaphalakaṁ agghati adhikasatasahassaṁ;
segs.e: However, this plank of sandalwood is worth over a thousand dollars.

segs.p: taṁ me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṁ upādāyā”ti.
segs.e: May the Buddha please accept it from me out of sympathy.”
So the Buddha accepted it out of sympathy.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā uggaṁ gahapatiṁ vesālikaṁ iminā anumodanīyena anumodi:
segs.e: And then the Buddha rejoiced with Ugga with these verses of appreciation:
“The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable,
enthusiastically giving clothing, bedding,
food and drink, and various requisites
to those of sincere conduct.
Knowing the perfected ones to be like a field
for what’s given, offered and not held back,
a true person gives what’s hard to give:
the giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā uggaṁ gahapatiṁ vesālikaṁ iminā anumodanīyena anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.
segs.e: And then the Buddha, having rejoiced with Ugga with these verses of appreciation, rose from his seat and left.

segs.p: Atha kho uggo gahapati vesāliko aparena samayena kālamakāsi.
segs.e: Then after some time Ugga passed away,

segs.p: Kālaṅkato ca uggo gahapati vesāliko aññataraṁ manomayaṁ kāyaṁ upapajji.
segs.e: and was reborn in a host of mind-made gods.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At that time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho uggo devaputto abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇo kevalakappaṁ jetavanaṁ obhāsetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṁ ṭhitaṁ kho uggaṁ devaputtaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then, late at night, the glorious godling Ugga, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. The Buddha said to him,
“Ugga, I trust it is all you wished?”
“Sir, it is indeed just as I wished.”

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā uggaṁ devaputtaṁ gāthāhi ajjhabhāsi:
segs.e: Then the Buddha addressed Ugga in verse:
“The giver of the agreeable gets the agreeable,
the giver of the foremost gets the foremost,
the giver of the excellent gets the excellent,
the giver of the best gets the best.
A person who gives the foremost,
the excellent, the best:
they’re long-lived and famous
wherever they’re reborn.”
Numbered Discourses 5.45
5. With King Muṇḍa
Overflowing Merit

segs.p: “Pañcime, bhikkhave, puññābhisandā kusalābhisandā sukhassāhārā sovaggikā sukhavipākā saggasaṁvattanikā iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya hitāya sukhāya saṁvattanti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, there are these five kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
What five?

segs.p: Yassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cīvaraṁ paribhuñjamāno appamāṇaṁ cetosamādhiṁ upasampajja viharati, appamāṇo tassa puññābhisando kusalābhisando sukhassāhāro sovaggiko sukhavipāko saggasaṁvattaniko iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya hitāya sukhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: When a mendicant enters and remains in a limitless immersion of the heart while using a robe …

segs.p: Yassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṁ paribhuñjamāno …pe… yassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vihāraṁ paribhuñjamāno …pe… yassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhu mañcapīṭhaṁ paribhuñjamāno …pe….
segs.e: almsfood … lodging … bed and chair …

segs.p: Yassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṁ paribhuñjamāno appamāṇaṁ cetosamādhiṁ upasampajja viharati, appamāṇo tassa puññābhisando kusalābhisando sukhassāhāro sovaggiko sukhavipāko saggasaṁvattaniko iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya hitāya sukhāya saṁvattati.
segs.e: medicines and supplies for the sick, the overflowing of merit for the donor is limitless …

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca puññābhisandā kusalābhisandā sukhassāhārā sovaggikā sukhavipākā saggasaṁvattanikā iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya hitāya sukhāya saṁvattanti.
segs.e: These are the five kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness, and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness, and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.

segs.p: Imehi ca pana, bhikkhave, pañcahi puññābhisandehi kusalābhisandehi samannāgatassa ariyasāvakassa na sukaraṁ puññassa pamāṇaṁ gahetuṁ:
segs.e: When a noble disciple has these five kinds of overflowing merit and goodness, it’s not easy to grasp how much merit they have by saying that

segs.p: ‘ettako puññābhisando kusalābhisando sukhassāhāro sovaggiko sukhavipāko saggasaṁvattaniko iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya hitāya sukhāya saṁvattatī’ti.
segs.e: this is the extent of their overflowing merit … that leads to happiness.

segs.p: Atha kho asaṅkheyyo appameyyo mahāpuññakkhandhotveva saṅkhaṁ gacchati.
segs.e: It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde na sukaraṁ udakassa pamāṇaṁ gahetuṁ:
segs.e: It’s like trying to grasp how much water is in the ocean. It’s not easy to say:

segs.p: ‘ettakāni udakāḷhakānīti vā ettakāni udakāḷhakasatānīti vā ettakāni udakāḷhakasahassānīti vā ettakāni udakāḷhakasatasahassānīti vā;
segs.e: ‘This is how many gallons, how many hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands of gallons there are.’

segs.p: atha kho asaṅkheyyo appameyyo mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhaṁ gacchati’.
segs.e: It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of water.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, imehi pañcahi puññābhisandehi kusalābhisandehi samannāgatassa ariyasāvakassa na sukaraṁ puññassa pamāṇaṁ gahetuṁ:
segs.e: In the same way, when a noble disciple has these five kinds of overflowing merit and goodness, it’s not easy to grasp how much merit they have:

segs.p: ‘ettako puññābhisando kusalābhisando sukhassāhāro sovaggiko sukhavipāko saggasaṁvattaniko iṭṭhāya kantāya manāpāya hitāya sukhāya saṁvattatī’ti.
segs.e: ‘This is how much this overflowing merit … leads to happiness.’

segs.p: Atha kho asaṅkheyyo appameyyo mahāpuññakkhandhotveva saṅkhaṁ gacchatīti.
segs.e: It’s simply reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
Hosts of people use the rivers,
and though the rivers are many,
all reach the great deep, the boundless ocean,
the cruel sea that’s home to precious gems.
So too, when a person gives food, drink, and clothes;
and they’re a giver of beds, seats, and mats—
the streams of merit reach that astute person,
as the rivers bring their waters to the sea.”
Numbered Discourses 5.46
5. With King Muṇḍa
Success
“Mendicants, there are five accomplishments.
What five?
Accomplishment in faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
These are the five accomplishments.”
Numbered Discourses 5.47
5. With King Muṇḍa
Wealth
“Mendicants, there are these five kinds of wealth.
What five?
The wealth of faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
And what is the wealth of faith?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako saddho hoti, saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṁ:
segs.e: It’s when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One’s awakening:

segs.p: ‘itipi so bhagavā …pe… satthā devamanussānaṁ buddho bhagavā’ti.
segs.e: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’
This is called the wealth of faith.
And what is the wealth of ethics?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti …pe… surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti.
segs.e: It’s when a noble disciple doesn’t kill living creatures, steal, commit sexual misconduct, lie, or consume intoxicants of beer, wine, and liquor.
This is called the wealth of ethics.
And what is the wealth of learning?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako bahussuto hoti …pe… diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdho.
segs.e: It’s when a noble disciple is very learned, remembering and keeping what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s totally full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reciting them, mentally scrutinizing them, and penetrating them theoretically.
This is called the wealth of learning.
And what is the wealth of generosity?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṁ ajjhāvasati muttacāgo payatapāṇi vosaggarato yācayogo dānasaṁvibhāgarato.
segs.e: It’s when a noble disciple lives at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.
This is called the wealth of generosity.
And what is the wealth of wisdom?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako paññavā hoti, udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā.
segs.e: It’s when a noble disciple is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.
This is called the wealth of wisdom.
These are the five kinds of wealth.
Whoever has faith in the Realized One,
unwavering and well grounded;
whose ethical conduct is good,
praised and loved by the noble ones;
who has confidence in the Saṅgha,
and correct view:
they’re said to be prosperous,
their life is not in vain.
So let the wise devote themselves
to faith, ethical behavior,
confidence, and insight into the teaching,
remembering the instructions of the Buddhas.”
Numbered Discourses 5.48
5. With King Muṇḍa
Things That Cannot Be Had

segs.p: “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, alabbhanīyāni ṭhānāni samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, there are five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.
What five?

segs.p: ‘Jarādhammaṁ mā jīrī’ti alabbhanīyaṁ ṭhānaṁ samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: That someone liable to old age should not grow old.

segs.p: ‘Byādhidhammaṁ mā byādhīyī’ti …pe… ‘maraṇadhammaṁ mā mīyī’ti … ‘khayadhammaṁ mā khīyī’ti … ‘nassanadhammaṁ mā nassī’ti alabbhanīyaṁ ṭhānaṁ samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: That someone liable to sickness should not get sick. … That someone liable to death should not die. … That someone liable to ending should not end. … That someone liable to perishing should not perish. …
An unlearned ordinary person has someone liable to old age who grows old.

segs.p: So jarādhamme jiṇṇe na iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: But they don’t reflect on old age:

segs.p: ‘na kho mayhevekassa jarādhammaṁ jīrati, atha kho yāvatā sattānaṁ āgati gati cuti upapatti sabbesaṁ sattānaṁ jarādhammaṁ jīrati.
segs.e: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to old age who grows old. For as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, they all have someone liable to old age who grows old.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana jarādhamme jiṇṇe soceyyaṁ kilameyyaṁ parideveyyaṁ, urattāḷiṁ kandeyyaṁ, sammohaṁ āpajjeyyaṁ, bhattampi me nacchādeyya, kāyepi dubbaṇṇiyaṁ okkameyya, kammantāpi nappavatteyyuṁ, amittāpi attamanā assu, mittāpi dummanā assū’ti.
segs.e: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to old age grows old, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

segs.p: So jarādhamme jiṇṇe socati kilamati paridevati, urattāḷiṁ kandati, sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: And so, when someone liable to old age grows old, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
This is called

segs.p: ‘assutavā puthujjano viddho savisena sokasallena attānaṁyeva paritāpeti’.
segs.e: an unlearned ordinary person struck by sorrow’s poisoned arrow, who only mortifies themselves.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, assutavato puthujjanassa byādhidhammaṁ byādhīyati …pe… maraṇadhammaṁ mīyati … khayadhammaṁ khīyati … nassanadhammaṁ nassati.
segs.e: Furthermore, an unlearned ordinary person has someone liable to sickness … death … ending … perishing.

segs.p: So nassanadhamme naṭṭhe na iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: But they don’t reflect on perishing:

segs.p: ‘na kho mayhevekassa nassanadhammaṁ nassati, atha kho yāvatā sattānaṁ āgati gati cuti upapatti sabbesaṁ sattānaṁ nassanadhammaṁ nassati.
segs.e: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to perishing who perishes. For as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, they all have someone liable to perishing who perishes.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana nassanadhamme naṭṭhe soceyyaṁ kilameyyaṁ parideveyyaṁ, urattāḷiṁ kandeyyaṁ, sammohaṁ āpajjeyyaṁ, bhattampi me nacchādeyya, kāyepi dubbaṇṇiyaṁ okkameyya, kammantāpi nappavatteyyuṁ, amittāpi attamanā assu, mittāpi dummanā assū’ti.
segs.e: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to perishing perishes, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

segs.p: So nassanadhamme naṭṭhe socati kilamati paridevati, urattāḷiṁ kandati, sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: And so, when someone liable to perishing perishes, they sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
This is called

segs.p: ‘assutavā puthujjano viddho savisena sokasallena attānaṁyeva paritāpeti’.
segs.e: an unlearned ordinary person struck by sorrow’s poisoned arrow, who only mortifies themselves.

segs.p: Sutavato ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa jarādhammaṁ jīrati.
segs.e: A learned noble disciple has someone liable to old age who grows old.
So they reflect on old age:

segs.p: ‘na kho mayhevekassa jarādhammaṁ jīrati, atha kho yāvatā sattānaṁ āgati gati cuti upapatti sabbesaṁ sattānaṁ jarādhammaṁ jīrati.
segs.e: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to old age who grows old. For as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, they all have someone liable to old age who grows old.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana jarādhamme jiṇṇe soceyyaṁ kilameyyaṁ parideveyyaṁ, urattāḷiṁ kandeyyaṁ, sammohaṁ āpajjeyyaṁ, bhattampi me nacchādeyya, kāyepi dubbaṇṇiyaṁ okkameyya, kammantāpi nappavatteyyuṁ, amittāpi attamanā assu, mittāpi dummanā assū’ti.
segs.e: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to old age grows old, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

segs.p: So jarādhamme jiṇṇe na socati na kilamati na paridevati, na urattāḷiṁ kandati, na sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: And so, when someone liable to old age grows old, they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
This is called

segs.p: ‘sutavā ariyasāvako abbuhi savisaṁ sokasallaṁ, yena viddho assutavā puthujjano attānaṁyeva paritāpeti.
segs.e: a learned noble disciple who has drawn out sorrow’s poisoned arrow, struck by which unlearned ordinary people only mortify themselves.
Sorrowless, free of thorns, that noble disciple only extinguishes themselves.

segs.p: Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa byādhidhammaṁ byādhīyati …pe… maraṇadhammaṁ mīyati … khayadhammaṁ khīyati … nassanadhammaṁ nassati.
segs.e: Furthermore, a learned noble disciple has someone liable to sickness … death … ending … perishing.
So they reflect on perishing:

segs.p: ‘na kho mayhevekassa nassanadhammaṁ nassati, atha kho yāvatā sattānaṁ āgati gati cuti upapatti sabbesaṁ sattānaṁ nassanadhammaṁ nassati.
segs.e: ‘It’s not just me who has someone liable to perishing who perishes. For as long as sentient beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, they all have someone liable to perishing who perishes.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana nassanadhamme naṭṭhe soceyyaṁ kilameyyaṁ parideveyyaṁ, urattāḷiṁ kandeyyaṁ, sammohaṁ āpajjeyyaṁ, bhattampi me nacchādeyya, kāyepi dubbaṇṇiyaṁ okkameyya, kammantāpi nappavatteyyuṁ, amittāpi attamanā assu, mittāpi dummanā assū’ti.
segs.e: If I were to sorrow and wail and lament, beating my breast and falling into confusion, just because someone liable to perishing perishes, I’d lose my appetite and my physical appearance would deteriorate. My work wouldn’t get done, my enemies would be encouraged, and my friends would be dispirited.’

segs.p: So nassanadhamme naṭṭhe na socati na kilamati na paridevati, na urattāḷiṁ kandati, na sammohaṁ āpajjati.
segs.e: And so, when someone liable to perishing perishes, they don’t sorrow and wail and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion.
This is called

segs.p: ‘sutavā ariyasāvako abbuhi savisaṁ sokasallaṁ, yena viddho assutavā puthujjano attānaṁyeva paritāpeti.
segs.e: a learned noble disciple who has drawn out sorrow’s poisoned arrow, struck by which unlearned ordinary people only mortify themselves.
Sorrowless, free of thorns, that noble disciple only extinguishes themselves.

segs.p: Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca alabbhanīyāni ṭhānāni samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasminti.
segs.e: These are the five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.
Sorrowing and lamenting
doesn’t do even a little bit of good.
When they know that you’re sad,
your enemies are encouraged.
When an astute person doesn’t waver <j>in the face of adversity,
as they’re able to evaluate what’s beneficial,
their enemies suffer,
seeing that their normal expression doesn’t change.
Prayers, recitations, fine sayings,
or charity of woven rugs:
if by means of any such things you benefit,
then by all means keep doing them.
But if you understand that ‘this good thing
can’t be had by me or by anyone else’,
you should accept it without sorrowing, thinking:
‘The deed is powerful. What can I do now?’”
Numbered Discourses 5.49
5. With King Muṇḍa
The King of Kosala

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

segs.p: Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
segs.e: Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena mallikā devī kālaṅkatā hoti.
Atha kho aññataro puriso yena rājā pasenadi kosalo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa upakaṇṇake āroceti:
segs.e: Then a man went up to the king and whispered in his ear,
“Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has passed away.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, rājā pasenadi kosalo dukkhī dummano pattakkhandho adhomukho pajjhāyanto appaṭibhāno nisīdi.
segs.e: When this was said, King Pasenadi was miserable and sad. He sat with his shoulders drooping, downcast, depressed, with nothing to say.

segs.p: Atha kho bhagavā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ dukkhiṁ dummanaṁ pattakkhandhaṁ adhomukhaṁ pajjhāyantaṁ appaṭibhānaṁ viditvā rājānaṁ pasenadiṁ kosalaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Knowing this, the Buddha said to him,

segs.p: “pañcimāni, mahārāja, alabbhanīyāni ṭhānāni samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṁ.
segs.e: “Great king, there are five things that cannot be had by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or divinity or by anyone in the world.
What five?

segs.p: ‘Jarādhammaṁ mā jīrī’ti alabbhanīyaṁ ṭhānaṁ …pe… na socanāya paridevanāya …pe… kammaṁ daḷhaṁ kinti karomi dānī”ti.
segs.e: That someone liable to old age should not grow old. … Sorrowing and lamenting doesn’t do even a little bit of good … ‘The deed is powerful. What can I do now?’”
Numbered Discourses 5.50
5. With King Muṇḍa
With Nārada

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ āyasmā nārado pāṭaliputte viharati kukkuṭārāme.
segs.e: At one time Venerable Nārada was staying near Pāṭaliputta, in the Chicken Monastery.

segs.p: Tena kho pana samayena muṇḍassa rañño bhaddā devī kālaṅkatā hoti piyā manāpā.
segs.e: Now at that time King Muṇḍa’s dear and beloved Queen Bhaddā had just passed away.

segs.p: So bhaddāya deviyā kālaṅkatāya piyāya manāpāya neva nhāyati na vilimpati na bhattaṁ bhuñjati na kammantaṁ payojeti—
segs.e: And since that time, the king did not bathe, anoint himself, eat his meals, or apply himself to his work.
Day and night he brooded over Queen Bhaddā’s corpse.

segs.p: Atha kho muṇḍo rājā piyakaṁ kosārakkhaṁ āmantesi:
segs.e: Then King Muṇḍa addressed Piyaka, the keeper of the treasury,

segs.p: “tena hi, samma piyaka, bhaddāya deviyā sarīraṁ āyasāya teladoṇiyā pakkhipitvā aññissā āyasāya doṇiyā paṭikujjatha, yathā mayaṁ bhaddāya deviyā sarīraṁ cirataraṁ passeyyāmā”ti.
segs.e: “So, my good Piyaka, please place Queen Bhaddā’s corpse in an iron casket filled with oil. Then close it up with another casket, so that we can view Queen Bhaddā’s body even longer.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, devā”ti kho piyako kosārakkho muṇḍassa rañño paṭissutvā bhaddāya deviyā sarīraṁ āyasāya teladoṇiyā pakkhipitvā aññissā āyasāya doṇiyā paṭikujji.
segs.e: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Piyaka, and he did as the king instructed.
Then it occurred to Piyaka,

segs.p: “imassa kho muṇḍassa rañño bhaddā devī kālaṅkatā piyā manāpā.
segs.e: “King Muṇḍa’s dear and beloved Queen Bhaddā has passed away.

segs.p: So bhaddāya deviyā kālaṅkatāya piyāya manāpāya neva nhāyati na vilimpati na bhattaṁ bhuñjati na kammantaṁ payojeti—
segs.e: Since then the king does not bathe, anoint himself, eat his meals, or apply himself to his work.
Day and night he broods over Queen Bhaddā’s corpse.

segs.p: Kaṁ nu kho muṇḍo rājā samaṇaṁ vā brāhmaṇaṁ vā payirupāseyya, yassa dhammaṁ sutvā sokasallaṁ pajaheyyā”ti.
segs.e: Now, what ascetic or brahmin might the king pay homage to, whose teaching could help the king give up sorrow’s arrow?”
Then it occurred to Piyaka,

segs.p: “ayaṁ kho āyasmā nārado pāṭaliputte viharati kukkuṭārāme.
segs.e: “This Venerable Nārada is staying in the Chicken Monastery at Pāṭaliputta.

segs.p: Taṁ kho panāyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ evaṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato:
segs.e: He has this good reputation:

segs.p: ‘paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho ceva arahā ca’.
segs.e: ‘He is astute, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, eloquent, mature, a perfected one.’

segs.p: Yannūna muṇḍo rājā āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ payirupāseyya, appeva nāma muṇḍo rājā āyasmato nāradassa dhammaṁ sutvā sokasallaṁ pajaheyyā”ti.
segs.e: What if King Muṇḍa was to pay homage to Venerable Nārada? Hopefully when he hears Nārada’s teaching, the king could give up sorrow’s arrow.”

segs.p: Atha kho piyako kosārakkho yena muṇḍo rājā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā muṇḍaṁ rājānaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Piyaka went to the king and said to him,

segs.p: “ayaṁ kho, deva, āyasmā nārado pāṭaliputte viharati kukkuṭārāme.
segs.e: “Your Majesty, this Venerable Nārada is staying in the Chicken Monastery at Pāṭaliputta.

segs.p: Taṁ kho panāyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ evaṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato:
segs.e: He has this good reputation:

segs.p: ‘paṇḍito viyatto medhāvī bahussuto cittakathī kalyāṇapaṭibhāno vuddho ceva arahā ca’.
segs.e: ‘He is astute, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, eloquent, mature, a perfected one.’

segs.p: Yadi pana devo āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ payirupāseyya, appeva nāma devo āyasmato nāradassa dhammaṁ sutvā sokasallaṁ pajaheyyā”ti.
segs.e: What if Your Majesty was to pay homage to Venerable Nārada? Hopefully when you hear Nārada’s teaching, you could give up sorrow’s arrow.”

segs.p: “Tena hi, samma piyaka, āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ paṭivedehi.
segs.e: “Well then, my good Piyaka, let Nārada know.

segs.p: Kathañhi nāma mādiso samaṇaṁ vā brāhmaṇaṁ vā vijite vasantaṁ pubbe appaṭisaṁvidito upasaṅkamitabbaṁ maññeyyā”ti.
segs.e: For how on earth could one such as I presume to visit an ascetic or brahmin in my realm without letting them know beforehand?”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, devā”ti kho piyako kosārakkho muṇḍassa rañño paṭissutvā yenāyasmā nārado tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho piyako kosārakkho āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Piyaka. He went to Nārada, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him,

segs.p: “Imassa, bhante, muṇḍassa rañño bhaddā devī kālaṅkatā piyā manāpā.
segs.e: “Sir, King Muṇḍa’s dear and beloved Queen Bhaddā has passed away.

segs.p: So bhaddāya deviyā kālaṅkatāya piyāya manāpāya neva nhāyati na vilimpati na bhattaṁ bhuñjati na kammantaṁ payojeti—
segs.e: And since she passed away, the king has not bathed, anointed himself, eaten his meals, or got his business done.
Day and night he broods over Queen Bhaddā’s corpse.

segs.p: Sādhu, bhante, āyasmā nārado muṇḍassa rañño tathā dhammaṁ desetu yathā muṇḍo rājā āyasmato nāradassa dhammaṁ sutvā sokasallaṁ pajaheyyā”ti.
segs.e: Sir, please teach the king so that, when he hears your teaching, he can give up sorrow’s arrow.”
“Please, Piyaka, let the king come at his convenience.”

segs.p: Atha kho piyako kosārakkho uṭṭhāyāsanā āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā yena muṇḍo rājā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā muṇḍaṁ rājānaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Piyaka rose from his seat, bowed, and respectfully circled Venerable Nārada, keeping him on his right, before going to the king and saying,
“Your Majesty, the request for an audience with Venerable Nārada has been granted.
Please, Your Majesty, go at your convenience.”

segs.p: “Tena hi, samma piyaka, bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojāpehī”ti.
segs.e: “Well then, my good Piyaka, harness the finest chariots.”

segs.p: “Evaṁ, devā”ti kho piyako kosārakkho muṇḍassa rañño paṭissutvā bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojāpetvā muṇḍaṁ rājānaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: “Yes, Your Majesty,” replied Piyaka. He did so, then told the king:

segs.p: “yuttāni kho te, deva, bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni.
segs.e: “Your Majesty, the finest chariots are harnessed.
Please, Your Majesty, go at your convenience.”

segs.p: Atha kho muṇḍo rājā bhadraṁ yānaṁ abhiruhitvā bhadrehi bhadrehi yānehi yena kukkuṭārāmo tena pāyāsi mahaccā rājānubhāvena āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ dassanāya.
segs.e: Then King Muṇḍa mounted a fine carriage and, along with other fine carriages, set out in full royal pomp to see Venerable Nārada at the Chicken Monastery.

segs.p: Yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi yānena gantvā, yānā paccorohitvā pattikova ārāmaṁ pāvisi.
segs.e: He went by carriage as far as the terrain allowed, then descended and entered the monastery on foot.

segs.p: Atha kho muṇḍo rājā yena āyasmā nārado tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ nāradaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho muṇḍaṁ rājānaṁ āyasmā nārado etadavoca:
segs.e: Then the king went up to Nārada, bowed, and sat down to one side. Then Nārada said to him:
